findings.quote:
# Resolve redirects if allowed.
        if allow_redirects:
            # Redirect resolving generator.
            gen = self.resolve_redirects(r, request, **kwargs)
            history = [resp for resp in gen]
findings.explanation: Session.send sends the initial PreparedRequest through adapter.send. Following mode exhausts resolve_redirects; each iteration copies the current request and source-level calls self.send with allow_redirects=False for one hop, avoiding recursive redirect handling. Non-following mode sends no redirect but invokes resolve_redirects with yield_requests=True once and stores the constructed request in Response._next. These are static call paths; because repository code and tests were not run, the concrete adapter or subclass methods selected by Python’s runtime dispatch are not empirically proven here.
For 303 and 302, every method except HEAD becomes GET. For 301, only POST becomes GET. HEAD and methods not covered by those conditions remain unchanged; therefore 307 and 308 preserve the method.

Only 307 Temporary Redirect and 308 Permanent Redirect retain the copied request’s body and entity headers. Every other followed redirect clears the body and removes Content-Length, Content-Type, and Transfer-Encoding, independently of whether rebuild_method changed the method.

For streaming data—an iterable excluding strings, lists, tuples, and mappings—preparation retains the stream as the body and records its current tell() position before transmission. An OSError from tell() stores a unique non-None sentinel so redirect handling attempts replay and reports an explicit rewind failure rather than silently reusing an exhausted stream.

Redirect handling calls this helper when _body_position is non-None and the retained headers contain Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding. Replay seeks to the recorded integer position. An OSError while seeking raises UnrewindableBodyError with the “error occurred” message; a missing seek method or non-integer position—including the failed-tell sentinel—raises UnrewindableBodyError saying the body is unable to rewind.

findings.explanation: Authorization is stripped whenever the hostname changes. On the same host, HTTP on an implicit/80 port may upgrade to HTTPS on an implicit/443 port without stripping. The same scheme also retains authorization when explicit default and omitted default ports are interchanged. Otherwise a scheme or port change strips it; an unchanged scheme and unchanged port—including the same non-default port—retains it.

findings.quote:
proxy_keys = [
        urlparts.scheme + "://" + urlparts.hostname,
        urlparts.scheme,
        "all://" + urlparts.hostname,
        "all",
    ]
findings.explanation: On every redirect, rebuild_proxies passes the new URL and current proxy map through resolve_proxies. That function copies the supplied map and, when trust_env is true and NO_PROXY does not bypass the target, adds the environment’s scheme-specific or all proxy using setdefault; an existing value for that same scheme key therefore wins. Selection priority is scheme-and-host, scheme, all-and-host, then all, so precedence across differently shaped keys follows that order. NO_PROXY prevents adding an environment proxy here, but this implementation does not delete proxy entries already present in the copied input map.

Each redirect unconditionally removes the copied Proxy-Authorization header. It examines the proxy URL stored under the redirected target’s scheme and recreates Basic proxy authorization only when both embedded username and password are truthy and the target scheme is not HTTPS. HTTPS omits this header to avoid leaking it through a tunnel; the standard adapter delegates proxy authentication there to urllib3.

findings.quote: r = adapter.send(request, **kwargs)
findings.explanation: Session.send sends the initial PreparedRequest through the adapter selected for its URL. With allow_redirects true it exhausts resolve_redirects; that generator copies each request and sends each hop through self.send(..., allow_redirects=False), preventing nested automatic following. With allow_redirects false, it sends only the current request, asks resolve_redirects in yield_requests mode for one prepared successor, and stores it in r._next without transmitting that successor. These are source-level dynamic calls: saved-graph caller queries found no resolved incoming edges for Session.send, resolve_redirects, or HTTPAdapter.send and explicitly marked runtime dispatch unverified, so the snapshot does not prove which subclass or mounted adapter implementation receives them at runtime.

For 303 and 302, every method except HEAD becomes GET. For 301, only POST becomes GET. HEAD remains HEAD, and methods not covered by those rules—including every method on 307 and 308—remain unchanged.

The copied body object and its headers are retained only for 307 Temporary Redirect and 308 Permanent Redirect. For the other automatically followed statuses—301, 302, and 303—the body is set to None and exactly Content-Length, Content-Type, and Transfer-Encoding are removed, even where the method policy left the method unchanged.

Preparation classifies an iterable that is not a string, list, tuple, or mapping as a stream. If its body has tell(), Requests records the current offset before transmission. An OSError from tell() stores a unique non-None sentinel rather than silently treating the body as non-rewindable. PreparedRequest.copy carries this value into redirected requests; streamed bodies also receive Content-Length when known or Transfer-Encoding: chunked otherwise.

resolve_redirects invokes this helper only when _body_position is non-None and the retained headers contain Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding. A seekable body with an integer recorded position is moved back to that offset. An OSError while seeking becomes UnrewindableBodyError with the specific rewinding message; a missing seek, non-integer position, or failed-tell sentinel raises UnrewindableBodyError saying the body cannot be rewound. Other seek exception types are not translated here.

findings.quote:
if old_parsed.hostname != new_parsed.hostname:
    return True
# Special case: allow http -> https redirect when using the standard
# ports.
if (
    old_parsed.scheme == "http"
    and old_parsed.port in (80, None)
    and new_parsed.scheme == "https"
    and new_parsed.port in (443, None)
):
    return False
findings.explanation: Authorization is eligible for retention only on the same hostname. On that host, Requests specially retains it for an HTTP default-port to HTTPS default-port upgrade. It also treats an omitted port and the scheme's explicit default port as equivalent when the scheme is unchanged. Otherwise a scheme or port change causes stripping; unchanged scheme and port retain authorization.

The copied Authorization header is deleted only when should_strip_auth rejects carrying it from the response's request URL to the redirect URL. Requests does not rerun the original explicit auth handler. Independently, when trust_env is enabled, credentials found in .netrc for the new URL are passed to prepare_auth and can recreate or replace the Authorization header.

Each redirect calls resolve_proxies with the new PreparedRequest and the proxy mapping carried from the preceding hop. That mapping is copied. If environment use is trusted and the new URL is not bypassed, an environment proxy for the target scheme—or its all fallback—is inserted only when that scheme key is absent. Thus an existing same-scheme value wins; bypassing suppresses environment insertion but does not remove existing explicit entries. Final proxy lookup prioritizes scheme://host, scheme, all://host, then all, as listed earlier in this range.

A copied Proxy-Authorization header is always removed. Requests then checks the newly resolved proxy URL under the target scheme for embedded credentials. It recreates a Basic proxy header only when both credentials are present and the target scheme is not HTTPS. For HTTPS targets it leaves the header absent so the standard adapter/urllib3 can handle tunnel authentication without exposing it to the destination.

# Handle redirection without scheme (see: RFC 1808 Section 4)
if url.startswith("//"):
    parsed_rurl = urlparse(resp.url)
    url = ":".join([to_native_string(parsed_rurl.scheme), url])

# Normalize url case and attach previous fragment if needed (RFC 7231 7.1.2)
parsed = urlparse(url)
if parsed.fragment == "" and previous_fragment:
    parsed = parsed._replace(fragment=previous_fragment)
elif parsed.fragment:
    previous_fragment = parsed.fragment
url = parsed.geturl()

# Facilitate relative 'location' headers, as allowed by RFC 7231.
# (e.g. '/path/to/resource' instead of 'http://domain.tld/path/to/resource')
# Compliant with RFC3986, we percent encode the url.
if not parsed.netloc:
    url = urljoin(resp.url, requote_uri(url))
else:
    url = requote_uri(url)
findings.explanation: Before another hop, Requests consumes resp.content (falling back to raw.read for decoding/chunk failures), raises TooManyRedirects once history reaches self.max_redirects, and normally closes the response to release the connection. A // target inherits the prior response's scheme; an omitted fragment inherits the previous fragment, while an explicit fragment becomes the new carried fragment. Relative targets are percent-requoted and joined to resp.url; absolute targets are requoted directly, then stored as native text. The loop continues only while get_redirect_target returns a Location for a recognized redirect response and terminates when it returns None; the configured redirect limit is the exceptional termination path.
